title: Warm winters raised next-summer counts of Swedish partial migrants in 1976-2025, but half of each gain reversed within two summers; winter warming explains about one third of the Wren increase
abstract: Question: do warmer winters increase next-summer bird counts in Sweden, and does this effect last long enough to change long-term trends? Data: Swedish Bird Survey fixed routes (597 routes, 1997-2025) and summer point routes (1,019 routes, 1976-2024), CC0; Swedish winter point counts classified each species as absent, partial or present in winter; E-OBS December-February temperature anomalies at each route. Method: same-observer changes between consecutive summers with route-year and species fixed effects, so summer migrants are the negative control; year-clustered errors and a year-relabel permutation test; a distributed-lag model gave the persistence of a one-winter effect. Results: a winter 1 C warmer than normal was followed by +1.10% (95% CI 0.57-1.64) and +0.92% (0.33-1.52) partial migrants relative to summer migrants in the two independent schemes (permutation p = 0.009 and 0.001). Fully winter-present species, many of them feeder seed-eaters, corvids and waterbirds, showed no clear effect (+0.37% and +0.08%). The placebo winter after the survey gave no effect. Species slopes agreed between schemes (r = 0.80); Wren had +11.5% and +7.6% per 1 C. About half of a class gain and most of a Wren gain reversed within two summers. With 0.55 C per decade of winter warming, the lasting effect predicts a small class trend difference (about 2% per decade), which the observed class trends did not show; it predicts about 35% of the Wren increase relative to summer migrants (upper limits 77-96%). Limitations: counts are indices without a detection model; the winter-presence ratio underestimates winter presence of songbirds; E-OBS has no snow data; species-level and Wren attribution are post hoc.
